subtype: Being let down by a broken promise [Receiver]
passage:
"Rukmini, I'm so sorry, beta. The meeting ran late."
"It's fine, Papa."
"How was the play? Did you get your lines right?"
"Yes."
"And the costume? Did your teacher like it?"
"I don't know. Maybe."
"Next time I'll definitely..."
"You said that at the science fair." She kept her eyes on her phone. "And sports day."
"That's not fair. I had work."
"I know. I'm not asking you to come any more. It's easier."
Her father, Amandeep, stood in the doorway. "Easier than what?"
"Than looking at the door the whole time." Her voice cracked on the last word, and she turned towards the wall.

qa.q: What two other events did Rukmini mention?
qa.a: Rukmini mentioned the science fair and sports day.

qa.q: What does Rukmini mean when she says it is easier not to ask?
qa.a: She means she has stopped hoping, because watching the door during the play hurt too much; she is protecting herself from more disappointment.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do now to begin repairing trust?
qa.a: He could stop defending himself, sit with her, admit the pattern, and make one small promise he truly keeps.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel standing in the doorway?
qa.a: He may feel shocked and guilty as he realises his broken promises have taught her to stop asking.

grounding: A teenage girl whose father keeps missing promised events takes it as proof she is not a priority and stops asking.

subtype: Being let down by a broken promise [Receiver]
passage:
I'm Madhuri, and I used to keep a list in the back of my notebook. Not chores. A list of "Amma will" things. Amma will come to the dance recital. Amma will take me to buy the blue kurta for my birthday. Amma will call on Sunday night.
Amma works long shifts at the hospital, and I know that. But one by one the list got crossed out, not by me, just by days passing. After my birthday I stopped adding things. When she asked, "What do you want this year?" I said, "Nothing, it's fine."
Last month my cousin Kavitha asked why I never tell Amma about my competitions. I didn't have an answer. I just didn't think asking would change anything any more.

qa.a: "Amma will" things: come to the dance recital, buy the blue kurta, call on Sunday night.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri stop adding to the list?
qa.a: After the birthday, Madhuri felt that asking wouldn't change anything, so hoping turned into protecting against disappointment.

qa.q: What could Madhuri try, even now?
qa.a: Madhuri could tell Amma calmly about the list and how it felt, giving Amma a chance to make one promise she can keep.

qa.q: How might Amma feel if she saw the crossed-out list?
qa.a: She would probably feel heartbroken and guilty, realising her long shifts had taught Madhuri to stop asking.

grounding: A teenager remembers a mother's repeated broken promises and how they taught Madhuri to stop hoping and stop asking.
